To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the concurrent application of SGS in NRS+patients might enhance the ability of NRS 2002 to predict poor clinical outcome in hospitalized patients in a Brazilian public university hospital.
the combination of NRS+ and the presence of SGA C is a more powerful predictor of poor clinical outcomes than either NRS+ or the presence of SGS C alone.
the concurrent application of S GA and NRS2002 in hospitalized patients might enhance their ability to predict poor outcomes in patients in Brazil.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of the NRS 2002 and SGA in hospitalized patients in a developing country.
the use of two nutritional assessment tools, SGA and NRS, in hospitalized adult patients.
the study of the complementarity of NRS 2002 and SGA for predicting VLLOS and death in hospitalized patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the concurrent application of SGS and NRS+ might enhance the ability of the SGA to predict poor clinical outcome in hospitalized patients.
the concurrent application of SAG in NRS+patients might enhance the ability of SGA to predict poor clinical outcome in hospitalized patients in the Brazilian setting.
SGA is more accurate in identifying the presence of malnutrition than the NRS, but that the combination of the two tools is more accurate in predicting poor clinical outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NRS+ and NRS+ SAG C patients are more likely to have complications than patients not at nutritional risks.
the NRS+ patients are at increased risk of complications, death and VLLOS.
NRS+ and malnutrition are associated with VLLOS and mortality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SGA is a more useful tool than NRS 2002 for predicting complications, VLLOS and death in patients with malnutrition.
NRS and SGA should be used concurrently to predict poor clinical outcome in hospitalized patients.
SGA is an important tool to be applied in patients with high nutritional risk (NNS 1.8).
